_comment: Route groups: ONE answer key, four frameworks. Feature 32.
RG-DEC-01 (converge): the prefix+path JOIN grammar diverged and was
UNGATED. PHP fully normalizes (Tina4/Router.php addRoute - the
reference: one separator, no double slash, a single leading slash, no
trailing slash). Python bare-concatenated (core/router.py, `path =
cls._group_prefix + path`), so group("/api") + get("users") silently
mis-registered at "/apiusers". Ruby's GroupContext bare-concatenated
("#{@prefix}#{path}") the same way. Node's RouteGroup did NO
normalization at all - the worst of the four, since its prefix isn't
even trailing-slash-trimmed on construction. Python/Ruby/Node now port
PHP's exact three-step grammar via ONE shared helper per language
(_join_group_path / join_group_path / joinGroupPath): join with one
separator, wrap to a single leading slash with no trailing slash, then
collapse any run of slashes to one. PHP needed no code change (it was
already correct) - this fixture proves PHP too, locking in the shared
contract rather than merely asserting the other three converged on it.
RG-DEC-02 (group-level auth parity): only Ruby's group() accepts a
group-level auth_handler: kwarg (dispatched for real since RG-03 was
corrected - dispatch_pipeline.rb). The owner ledger (OWNER-DECISIONS.md
Batch 4) ratifies ONLY the slash-normalization convergence for feature
32 - it does not require a group-level auth declaration surface in
Python/PHP/Node. This is documented as a Ruby-only convenience, not a
security gap: writes are secure-by-default in all four regardless of
group middleware (RG-04, the write-auth-gate invariant below), with or
without a group-level auth_handler. No new surface was added to
Python/PHP/Node.
Every case is driven through a REAL request pipeline: Python's
TestClient (-> core.server.app, the real front controller), PHP's
TestClient (-> Router::dispatch), Ruby's TestClient (->
Tina4::RackApp#call) all dispatch with NO mocks; Node boots a REAL
server (startServer) and makes REAL HTTP requests over a real socket.
The four suites carry the SAME case names in each language's own idiom
(Python snake_case method, PHP testPascalCase method, Ruby it-
description, Node assert label), which
scripts/audit-contract-fixtures.py normalises and matches.
Mutation-proved (Python, Ruby, Node): reverting each language's fix
back to its old bare concatenation reds exactly
group_prefix_joins_to_a_single_slash_path and
nested_groups_concatenate_the_prefix (Node additionally reds
trailing_slash_on_the_prefix_is_normalized, since it never trimmed the
group prefix at all) - restored and re-verified green.

invariants.rule: group(prefix) + get(path) where path carries NO leading slash (e.g. group("/api") + get("users")) registers at the single-separator canonical path "/api/users" - not the bare-concatenation mis-registration "/apiusers".
invariants.why: RG-SLASH-NORMALIZE: Python bare-concatenated cls._group_prefix + path with no separator logic; Ruby's GroupContext did the same ("#{@prefix}#{path}"); Node's RouteGroup did the same (this.prefix + path). A route silently mis-registered at the wrong path in three of four languages, and no slash test existed in any language before this feature.

invariants.rule: group(prefix) + get(path) where path ALREADY carries its own leading slash (e.g. group("/api") + get("/users")) ALSO registers at "/api/users" - the identical canonical path the no-leading-slash form resolves to, never a doubled separator ("/api//users").
invariants.why: A naive fix that always inserts a separator without first stripping the route's own leading slash would introduce a NEW double-slash regression. Proving this case alongside the bare-concat case (route-groups-prefix-joins-single-slash) locks the join grammar to converge on ONE canonical path regardless of which form the developer writes.

invariants.rule: group(prefix) where prefix carries a trailing slash (e.g. group("/api/") + get("/users")) ALSO registers at "/api/users" - the SAME canonical path, never a doubled separator ("/api//users").
invariants.why: RG-SLASH-NORMALIZE named this exact repro for Ruby ("chomp strips only ONE trailing slash") and it is unguarded in Node (no trailing-slash trim on the group prefix at all - Node reds this case under mutation while Python/Ruby do not, since Node's RouteGroup constructor never trimmed the prefix to begin with).

invariants.rule: Nested groups compose the prefix through the SAME normalized join: group("/api") > group("/v1") + get("users") registers at "/api/v1/users" - not the missing-separator mis-registration "/api/v1users".
invariants.why: The prefix-join bug is not confined to a single group level - the innermost route's own path still needs the same one-separator join against the fully-composed nested prefix. Proven with a real nested registration, not merely asserted from the single-level case.

invariants.rule: Attaching an ordinary (non-auth) middleware to a route group NEVER disables the secure-by-default write-auth gate - a tokenless POST to a grouped route still 401s, including under the newly-normalized prefix join.
invariants.why: The one SECURITY-relevant property of this feature. Feature 79's RG-04 already locked this in all four (Python router.py, PHP Router.php, Ruby router.rb, Node router.ts); this case re-proves it specifically against the route_groups_contract fixture scope, under the new normalization, so the slash-join fix is never reported done at the cost of quietly reopening RG-04.

invariants.rule: A route path containing a literal regex metacharacter (`(` `)` `.` `+` `?` `[` etc.) matches ONLY that literal path - the router's pattern compiler quotes every literal segment before it reaches the compiled regex, and only the {param}/{param:type} placeholder syntax becomes a capture group.
invariants.why: CONFIRMED broken in PHP and Node.js: both compiled a literal path segment straight into the final regex pattern UNESCAPED, so a metacharacter changed what the pattern actually matched. Registering `/blocked-xss(1)` compiled the trailing `(1)` as a REGEX CAPTURE GROUP, so the compiled pattern required the URL WITHOUT the parens - the exact literal path the route was registered for 404'd on the exact request for it. Isolated to metacharacters (not letters/digits/hyphens); a `.` in a path segment behaved as a regex any-char wildcard instead of a literal dot, an overly-loose-match footgun of the same defect. Python (`re.escape`) and Ruby (`Regexp.escape`) already quoted every literal segment correctly - CODE WINS there, empirically re-proven here, not merely re-read from source.
